The rest of the section, I think, is a consolidation of the old Act except that there is a new provision here. I would like to read it and ask the minister if he has any comment to make. y
Provided that where the deputy returning officer has inadvertently omitted to remove the counterfoil from the ballot paper before placing such ballot paper in the ballot box, he may, exercising care however that the number on such counterfoil be not seen by any person present and without himself examining such number, remove and destroy such counterfoil at the counting of the ballots; and the judge who may conduct any recount proceedings shall have the like power, inadvertence on the part of the deputy returning officer being, for the purposes of the recount, presumed. The ballots, if otherwise in proper form, shall be counted as if the counterfoil had been at the proper time removed therefrom.
What is the significance of that proviso?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The proviso is drawn by Mr. W. F. O'Connor, K.C., who had a good deal to do with the drafting of the Bill, In the history of election matters it has been found in quite a number of instances, that through inadvertence, the returning officer on receiving the ballot from the voter will place it in the ballot box without removing the counterfoil. When a recount takes place the question arises whether this is or is not a spoiled ballot. It would be wrong to deprive a man of his vote through the inadvertence of the returning officer, and if the returning officer should remove the counterfoil without exposing the ballot, it would be considered a good ballot. A like consideration would apply before a judge engaged in the making of a recount. I have known of cases in recounts where ballots are found with the counterfoil attached. I remember that on one occasion a judge held in one place that those ballots were good

votes, whilst another judge in the next county held that they were not good votes. It is to remove any doubt upon that question, in order that a man who has honestly voted shall not be deprived of his vote from any inadvertence on the part of the returning officer.

rural polling divisions?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In form AA if the voter's name is on the list of voters.
Very well then, form BB.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That could only apply
to a man whose name is not on the voters' list.

Do I understand that
a man may vote in rural subdivisions even if his name is not on the list?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The ballot goes into the box just the same.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have not reached the section dealing with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No. It is section 63, we will come to it.

From the reading of subsection (6) of this clause together with subsection (1) of section 60, paragraph (c), one might understand that the ballot proper is going to be numbered. Is that the purpose of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The counterfoil is numbered, not the ballot paper. The ballot paper itself is stamped and initialled. It is the duty of the deputy returning officer to tear that counterfoil off. Then it is destroyed.

It is not to be numbered but it reads as if it were to be numbered. Although wre have passed section 60 let us read these two sections together. Let us take paragraph (c) of section 60 which reads as follows:
-at the counting of the votes attempt to ascertain the number on the back of any ballot paper.
How can there be a number on the back of a ballot paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Unless it was inadvertently put in by the deputy returning officer.

I would suggest to the minister that the paragraph should be made clearer. As it reads now, if a man were not perfectly well aware that the ballot should not bear a number on its back, the wording might make one believe that it should be numbered.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is a number in the case where a man goes to the poll and finds somebody else has voted in his name. There is a number put on and that is entered in the poll book. That is provided .for in the clause under consideration, clause 62.
In that ease the man's vote is not . a secret any longer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is pretty secret,

No, it is not secret. Suppose Jack Smith enters the polling place and you give him ia ballot that is numbered 100. The ballot is put in the box and afterwards the box is opened and it is found that the number 100 is on the ballot of Jack Smith; then it is no longer secret.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Would you deprive that man of his vote or would you identify the vote? I do not want to deprive that man of his vote. If I go to the polling place and find some one has voted in my name I do not want to be deprived of my vote.

At the same time I take the oath and I get a ballot. Now there is <a provision that the ballot I get has a number on the back of it. That is for the purpose of identity. Every precaution is taken with regard to .secrecy and everybody is sworn in connection with it.
(Mr. ROSS: Why is it necessary to identify that man after he has been sworn once?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It may subsequently be
a question whether I have a right to vote or the other man. I might not be known at the polls.

I cannot see any object in
it.	t

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My vote may be questioned. How are you going to find the ballot unless there is a number on it? I come up and say: I am John Smith. The deputy returning officer tells me that John Smith has already voted. I deny that the right John Smith has voted, and I take the oath. Thus there are two ballots for John Smith. The numbered ballot identifies me in case of a recount. It may be that a man has fraudulently voted.

In that case is there
any question of the bona fide character of -the vote? And if there is none why identity it?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It may be honest and
bona fide. I might be the proper one to poll the vote, or I might not be; I might be the fraudulent person.
That is to be established at a recount? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In case a recount became necessary. It is a thing that would not happen very often, but I think there should be some way of checking it up.

If either man has not
been identified you have to identity the man who had the honest vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well identify one or
the other.

The first man to vote
might not be the fraudulent voter.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
To my mind this is a
safeguard but I am not going to press the point.
. Mr. ARTHURS: It has always been the rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It was copied from the
old law. If any one objects to the provision, let it go.

In case a fraudulent
vote the identity would be discovered by the number on the back of the ballot?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The judge would identify the ballot voted by John Smith.

Would the ballot be
thrown out?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If it were proven that
John Smith voted fraudulently and was not the actual John Smith who had a right to vote the ballot would certainly be thrown out. If it was proven that the right man had voted on the numbered ballot it would be counted.

Suppose the wrong
man voted first what would be done about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot help you there. We cannot stop up every gap for fraud.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Section 63 had better stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that section
63 stand.,
Motion agreed to: section stands.
On section 64-peace and good order at elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is an error in subsection 2 at line 13. The words "Chief Electoral" should be struck out, and the word "Returning" inserted. I move that amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Subsection 2 of this section is entirely new, is it not? Is there any special reason for this addition?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a new clause, and I think it is a very useful one. With the amendment I propose it would read:
Constab'es sha'.l be appointed to act at polling stations only in cases where the returning officer fears that otherwise disorder will result thereat. In cities and towns returning officers may provide, and locate during polling day at convenient places, one or more posses of three or more constables each, as may be authorized by the Returning Officer, with means of information and of quick conveyance to any place where the services of such posses may be required.
This is just an extra safeguard. If anyone fears a riot or an unfair election there is power to take preventive measures.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister now suggests to make the clause read:
In cities and towns returning officers may provide and locate during polling day at convenient places, one or more posses of three or

more constables each, as may be authorize*} by the Returning Officer.
I think the change makes the clause rather different from what he intended.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The Returning Officer is on the spot, he has general control of the whole constituency, and he may know of conditions which lead him to fear a riot or other disturbance; the Chief Electoral Officer is here in Ottawa. I think the discretion should be invested in some one on the spot.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But the clause as now amended reads that in cities and towns returning officers may provide and locate one or more posses as may be authorized by the returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Oh yes. I should have moved, Mr. Chairman, that the words "as may be authorized by the Chief Electoral Officer" be stricken out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Then I think to make the language of this section conform with that of many other sections we should add the words "and incorporated villages." In other sections wherever the phrase occurs it is in the form of "cities, towns and incorporated villages." I would therefore move that the words "and incorporated villages" be inserted after the word "towns" in line ten, and that the word "and" before "towns" be struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

In connection with subsection 2 I see a decided objection to the language of the first sentence:
Constables shall be appointed to act at polling stations only in cases where the returning officer fears that otherwise disorder will result thereat.
In many constituencies, particularly in the outlying districts, the returning officer is many males away from the polling subdivision, and it would be absolutely impossible for him to have any personal knowledge of the situation. The deputy returning officer would be the man with knowledge of local conditions. I suggest that the word "deputy" be inserted before "returning officer."
Is this taken from the English Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We give every poll clerk the authority of a constable, and every deputy returning officer has the authority of a justice of the peace. Then by way of 
extra precaution the returning officer is empowered to provide a posse.

We have always had that authority vested in the poll dlerk and the deputy returning officer, but we have also always had a constable at these polls. Take any part of Northern Ontario or Western Canada, the returning officer does not know the local conditions at all, and a difficult situation may arise very suddenly.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is another safeguard provided. Any candidate or his agent, or any two electors, may require any returning officer or deputy returning officer to swearvin such special constables as he deems^ necessary. I think there is ample provision for appointing constables.
Is it intended that a constable shall be appointed at everv polling station?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, not necessarily.

I would like to have some information in reference to subsection 5, which reads:
Upon receiving the information the deputyreturning officer may, on the polling day, but not afterwards, issue his warrant in form FF or GG, as the case may be, for the arrest of the person charged, in order that he may be brought before the magistrate,-
And so on. Surely the voting at the polls should not be held up in order that the deputy returning officer may be enabled to issue his warrant.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This also is merely an extra precaution. If a man wants to go to another magistrate there is nothing to prevent his doing so. But in case another magistrate is not available and quick action is necessary, authority is given to the deputy to issue at once a warrant for the arrest of the person charged. It would not take more than a moment to write out a warrant for a, man's arrest. In any case, if there is a desire not to interrupt the deputy returning officer any one can take the ordinary process of law and go before another magistrate. The object of this is to have action taken on the spot so that the offender may not vote and get away.

Deputy returning officers
are not all lawyers; they may want to take time to get the warrant in shape. The polling might be delayed half an hour, and that would be most undesirable.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does the minister think that that power should be taken away? .

Subsection 3 reads:
If a person Is charged at a polling station with having committed the offence of personation.
An evil-minded person who enters the polling booth with the intention of impersonating another voter may be detected before he carries out his intention. Under this section there is no power to deal with such a case. It seems to me that the provision should cover also an attempt to commit the offence of personation; the result would be a tendency to prevent the evil-minded person from entering the booth at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to
amending the section accordingly, if the committee is of that opinion. I move that section 64 be further amended by inserting in line 18, page 45, after the word " committed " the words "or attempted to commit", and by adding after the word "voted" in line 18, the words "or attempted to vote".

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Unless the minister can give some substantial reason why subsection 2 should remain in the Bill, it seems to me that it should be struck out. The effect of it is that in any incorporated village, town or city the returning officer may have groups of three men as special constables, posses of police, wandering about during the day of the election in the vicinity of polls. That would mean a considerable amount of government patronage, and it would open the door to corruption and to an element of terrorizing in some communities rather than the opposite. I think it would be much wiser to return to the old law, unless there is some substantial reason why we should introduce this police system at our elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am not wedded to the proposal. If my hon. friend moves to strike it out, I agree.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I move to strike out subsection 2.

-It is unfair to assume
that in case of disorder at a polling subdivision the constables would be at the beck and call only of the Government officials. They would be there, I should thipk, for the purpose of preserving order for all the people and to ensure a proper and fair election for everybody; and to strike out this provision would not tend to ensure the conduct of elections in the manner desired by every law-abiding citizen. As to the question of
patronage, I suppose that is a case of honi soit qui mal y pense.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Under another subsection there is power to appoint as many constables as necessary. This is only an extra precaution, a provision to afford a greater safeguard in the case of disturbance, but I cannot see that it very much improves the old law.
Every city, town and village have their own police forces which could be called upon in case of riot or disturbance. I do not see any necessity for subsection 2.
Surely subsection 8 gives ample power to the proper officers and affords necessary precautions for cases of that kind.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Re-numbering of the subsections follows as a matter of course.

In subsection 1, it is provided that when a person has been arrested during polling day, the order for his arrest will not hold good after the close of the poll. If a deputy returning officer wants to lodge a complaint against a person who has been arrested by him during the day, he should be given some time after the closing of the poll to prepare and lodge his complaint, but under this subsection the person arrested would be set free at six o'clock. Why not say that such order signed by the deputy returning officer shall hold good until nine or ten o'clock of the same night, in order to give the deputy returning "officer some time in which to lodge a complaint if he wants to do so? Until six o'clock the deputy returning officer is engaged and consequently is unable to prepare and lodge such a complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This is a very old clause and I do not know that much would be gained by amending it. To keep a man, who may probably be innocent, locked up all day without sending him before a magistrate, would be dealing very harshly with him.

Subsection 8 reads:
Every poll clerk shall have the authority of a constable for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of this Act respecting summary proceedings in cases of personation.
Why should he not have that authority in every case and not merely in a case of personation?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This clause has stood the test of time and I do not see that much is to be gained by amending it.
In ease of any trouble m a poll, should not the poll clerk have the authority of a constable?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There are always plenty of constables round a poll and I would not favour the amendment.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 65-strangers not to enter polling districts armed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Subsection 5 has a few additions of which I do not know just the significance. After the words " no spirituous or fermented liquors " there have been added the words " whether or not intoxicating." This addition looks as if it had been put in by the Minister of Health. The subsection states further:
-shall he sold or given at any hotel, tavern, shop or other place within the limits of any polling division, before, during or after the hours during which the poll is open on polling day.
The words " before " and " or after " have also been added. This is really prohibition legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is meant to allow two per cent and to exclude four per cent, whereas, in the opinion of a good many people, four per cent is not intoxicating.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is meant by " before or after " the hours of polling?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The old law always was that shops and taverns should be closed the whole of polling day; no liquor was allowed to be sold, and I suppose this was intended to carry out that idea.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The old law was that no liquor should be sold during the hours during which the poll was open on polling day. The words that have been added are " before or after ". That practically makes it impossible to sell these drinks at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That was always the law.
When you change the time between nomination and polling day, why do you not change this to fourteen days instead of eight?
As regards the phrase " whether or not intoxicating," I should like to have a definition of the term " intoxicating." I have never yet come across one which would stand the test of criticism.

Another objection to this clause is that it is so drastic that a man 
could not accept from his tvife in his own home after a hard day's work at the election, a small portion of stimulant that might prevent him from going into a serious state of collapse. This is going about as far as any legislation could go towards something that is not now prohibited by any law that is in existence. Under this subclause, a man could not, between five o'clock in the morning and twelve o'clock at night of polling day, accept off his own sideboard, at the hands of any person, whether a member of his family or not, a glass of wine which is intoxicating.
Not even to drown his sorrow.

I was not thinking of that; I was speaking more about the drastic nature of the clause as affecting the liberty of the subject. We ought to be rather chary about going in an Election Act further than is gone in
9 p.m. any other Act of which I know. There are many other drastic measures in force to-day and the public are complaining against them. It would be well if we had fewer restrictions and a little relaxation from the drastic effects of these public Acts. I think it would meet the approval of the best citizens if this subsection were struck out altogether. Let us not be abnormally drastic about measures that go to the root of the social customs of the people.

If it was thought advisable
to increase the time between nomination day and polling day to fourteen days, would it not be logical to increase the time during which these restrictions shall apply from eight to fourteen days also?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there was any logic in the matter at all. The time fixed in this section was considered an adequate period during which to forbid the use of badges. Eight days is long enough, and in any event I do not think there is very much in the matter one way or another. In regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) concerning subsection 5, I would suggest that the words " whether or not intoxicating " be struck out, and the words " public place" be substituted for the words " or other place". I do not. think we should go the length of going into a man's house.

The subsection
says that no liquor shall be sold during or after the hours during which the poll is open on polling day. The day starts at

midnight preceding. The prohibition should start with the commencement of the polling day.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That was always the
law; for the whole twenty-four hours of [DOT]election day the sale of liquor was prohibited.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the
advantage of adding the words " whether or not intoxicating " or the words " before, during or after "? If the prohibition is to [DOT]apply during the whole of polling day these words are unnecessary; and if you retain the words " whether or not intoxicating," you would prohibit the use of ginger beer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that subsection 5 be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
No spiritous or ifermented liquors or strong drinks shall he sold or given at any hotel, tavern, shop or other place within the limits of any polling division during the whole of the polling day at any election.

I repeat the objection I raised to the clause as it stood before, and I would ask the minister to insert before the word " place " the word " public," or to adopt some other language that will safeguard the liberty of a man's home.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think we should adopt the section as amended.
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
On section 66-counting and reporting the vote:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There are some clerical errors in that clause. On page 47, line 3, the word " defaced " appears. Throughout the other sections the word " spoiled " is used. I beg to move:
That clause 66 be amended by striking out the word " defaced " in line 28, and substitute the word " spoiled."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
On page 48, subsection
7 it says: " This large envelope shall be sealed." I beg to move:
That the word " then " be inserted after the word " shall '' in the 51st line, page 48.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Subsections 8 and 9 are new, and with that exception this is practically a repetition of the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Subsections 8 and 9 are good subsections.
Mr. GUTHRIE; There is little change in the language but it is really a consolidation of the old sections.
There is some qualification about Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is omitted from
this section.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

In subsection 8 it is
provided that the ballot box shall " be carried free in the Canadian mails as registered matter." It occurred to me that under the regulations that might involve the delay of a day unless the words were added " by special delivery." Under the regulations with reference to registered matter you practically lose a day because notice is given on "one day and the parcel is sent the next.	*	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I like the old section.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is just one point in connection with the suggestion that the hon. member (Mr. Morphy) has made. The provision about the ballot box being carried as registered matter seems to have been put in for the purpose of safety and security in delivery. If you introduce the words " special delivery " it will take the ballot box out of the hands of those persons specially entrusted with registered matter and put it in the hands of messengers who are simply handling special delivery matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think if it goes by
registered mail it would be satisfactory. I believe that we can expect the Post Office Department to deliver the boxes [DOT] with reasonable speed.

.Subsection 1 of
section 66 provides that the ballots shall be counted in the presence of at least three electors. Is that a provision that has always been in effect under the old law?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It has been in effect
for a long time.
It has not been carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As a rule there have
been more than that present where I live.

speechtext:
This section
is identical with the old Act, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There are one or two
clerical errors here. In line 28, page 52, appear the words "several returning officers." It should be "several deputy returning officers." I move that the change be made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speechtext:

there is a reference to section 66. It should be section 67.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There was
some reference in the old Act, section 193, to the judges of the Superior Courts of Saskatchewan and Alberta. That reference is omitted in this clause, and I would ask if there is any significance in the change.
' Mr. GUTHRIE:	In Saskatchewan they
have both Superior Court and District Court judges. The District Court judges correspond as nearly as possible with the County Court judges in the province of Ontario. It is to the District Court judges that these recounts go, and in the province of Ontario to the County Court judges. A different system is in vogue in the province of Quebec. There they have no County Court judges, and the recounts in that province go to the Superior Court judges. The proper officials now to conduct the recount in the .province of Saskatchewan would be the District Court judges.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What about
Alberta?

speechtext: Alberta is the same now.
I would ask the minister why he left out section 201 in the old Act which provides that the judge may review the decision of a returning officer in case of the loss of a ballot box.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 201 is in as part of subsection 4:
He shall also, it necessary or requires, review the decision of the returning officer with respect to the number of votes given for a candidate, etc.
There has been a re-arrangement of the old sections, but I think the sense and the language have been very well preserved.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Sections 99 and 201 of the old Act are combined?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.

speechtext: Is it the desire of the committee that this clause be read?

speechtext: It is purely formal.

speechtext: Are there any clerical errors in it?

On section 72-election return:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How longTs
it going to take a candidate to get back his deposit under subsection 5?

speechtext:

Mr. FIELDING. This question arose on a previous section.

whether my hon. friend gave us any parti' cular reason why we should depart from the present practice whereby the returning officer pays over the money to the candidate.

That is all

On section 76-fees and expenses of election officers:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the significance of the italics in subsection 5?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that we shall have to place a resolution on the Order Paper in regard to the payment of these fees after the Bill goes through committee and before it is read the third time.
I should like to direct the attention of the minister to some of these fees in the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, we have not yet come to that. This section will have to stand until the resolution is adopted.
Section 76 stands.
On section 77-how disagreements as to taxation of expenses settled:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Gisborne and the Auditor General have discussed the matter of this provision and have drafted a new clause. If it meets with the approval of the committee I suggest that it be substituted for the present section 77. It reads as follows:
The Auditor General shall, in accordance with this Act, tax and pay all election expense accounts. Any disagreement between the Auditor General and any claimant shall be referred to the Chief Electoral Officer and he shall either confirm the action of th^ Auditor General, or if he disagrees, then, if the question involves only the legal right of a person claiming payment to be paid at all, it shall be referred to and be finally resolved by the Treasury Board, or if the question involves only the fairness of the amount payable to any person with relation to the services or materials supplied, it shall be referred to and shall be finally resolved by the Secretary of State. Notwithstanding anything in this section contained the rights, if any, of all claimants to compel payment or further payment by a process of law shall remain unimpaired.
I admit that that is a practical solution of the difficulty, but is it not a departure from the whole theory upon which the work of the Auditor General is based?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I agree that it is a departure, but the practice has grown up of having election accounts actually taxed by the Auditor General. In some outlying constituencies the accounts are rather heavy and difficulty has arisen in connection witn their adjustment. When this Bill was drafted it was proposed to allow the Chief Electoral Officer and the Auditor General to adjust these accounts, but, as I have stated a new clause was drafted as the result of a conference between the Auditor General and the Chief Electoral Officer.

I suggest that the Chief Electoral Officer should tax the accounts, which then would be subject to review by the Auditor General. The Chief Electoral Officer is a better judge of what has happened than the Auditor General. The Auditor General knows nothing about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes, he does.

During the last election many disputes arose throughout the country in connection with the expenses of the election. Some cases of considerable hardship to the returning officers occurred in the province from which I come. There is a provision in the law which requires a notice to be put up with the proclamation. Proclamations were sent out from the Dominion elections officer in Ottawa without that notice. Discovery of the omission was made later, and telegrams were sent to returning officers all over Canada instructing them that if the proclamations had not been put up, these notices should now go with them, and that in cases where they had been put up, the notices should be put up as well. But when the accounts came in the Auditor General would not pay for the putting up of the second notice, though in some of the outlying districts a good deal of money was spent in that connection. Can the minister say whether these disputed-accounts have been settled?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have no knowledge of the matter.	.

I cannot recall any case where the Auditor General has been treated as an executive officer. The theory upon which the Auditor General works is that he is the watchdog of the treasury. He does not initiate anything, but all expenses come under his review, and if they do not meet with his favour he vetos them if possible, or if the amount has been paid he makes a note of the matter in his bluebook; this is brought down to Parliament and if we agree with him we call the Government to account. To make him an executive officer

may be the only way out of the difficulty, but theoretically it is not right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am not positive, but I am inclined to think that the Auditor General has for a long time taxed the allowances and expenses of judges.

In the sense that all
these things come under his review.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is my impression that he actually fixes them. I have heard some complaints on the subject, but this provision would be along the same line.
Mr. GLASS':	There might be some improved machinery for the adjusting of these election accounts. In many cases there has been hardship as well as a great deal of bitter feeling and dissatisfaction in this connection. They have to pass under the purview of one person who has many other duties to perform, and many months elapse before they are adjusted; sometimes it takes even more than a year. The returning officer has in some cases as many as 65 or 70 deputies; each of these has poll clerks and other officials, and all payments to these different officials are held up until one man at headquarters at Ottawa can adjust the details of accounts from some 235 constituencies.
The machinery has not been adequate to meet promptly the needs in connection with the adjustment of these matters. If it were possible, as the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) suggested, that some other competent official had delegated to him the passing of these accounts, tvith .the Auditor General acting as the watchdog and auditing them for him afterwards, that would result in a very much more speedy adjustment of these accounts and would give better satisfaction to the thousands of officials who have to act in connection with a federal election.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Had not this clause better stand for further consideration? I should like to point out to my hon. friend that the next few clauses contain a good deal of entirely new legislation; they are copied from the English Act and the like, and they are very long clauses. There are only about a baker's dozen of my hon. friend's friends on the other side, and it is pretty late; we have done a lot of work on this measure to-day and I think we should adjourn.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
